title: Dijkstra Algorithm
html:
You are given a directed or undirected weighted graph with nnn vertices and mmm edges. The weights of all edges are non-negative. You are also given a starting vertex sss. This article discusses finding the lengths of the shortest paths from a starting vertex sss to all other vertices, and output the shortest paths themselves.

This problem is also called single-source shortest paths problem.

Algorithm

Here is an algorithm described by the Dutch computer scientist Edsger W. Dijkstra in 1959.

Let's create an array d[]d[]d[] where for each vertex vvv we store the current length of the shortest path from sss to vvv in d[v]d[v]d[v]. Initially d[s]=0d[s] = 0d[s]=0, and for all other vertices this length equals infinity. In the implementation a sufficiently large number (which is guaranteed to be greater than any possible path length) is chosen as infinity.

d[v]=∞, v≠sd[v] = \infty,~ v \ne sd[v]=∞, v=s

In addition, we maintain a Boolean array u[]u[]u[] which stores for each vertex vvv whether it's marked. Initially all vertices are unmarked:

u[v]=falseu[v] = {\rm false}u[v]=false

The Dijkstra's algorithm runs for nnn iterations. At each iteration a vertex vvv is chosen as unmarked vertex which has the least value d[v]d[v]d[v]:

Evidently, in the first iteration the starting vertex sss will be selected.

The selected vertex vvv is marked. Next, from vertex vvv relaxations are performed: all edges of the form (v,to)(v,\text{to})(v,to) are considered, and for each vertex to\text{to}to the algorithm tries to improve the value d[to]d[\text{to}]d[to]. If the length of the current edge equals lenlenlen, the code for relaxation is:

d[to]=min⁡(d[to],d[v]+len)d[\text{to}] = \min (d[\text{to}], d[v] + len)d[to]=min(d[to],d[v]+len)

After all such edges are considered, the current iteration ends. Finally, after nnn iterations, all vertices will be marked, and the algorithm terminates. We claim that the found values d[v]d[v]d[v] are the lengths of shortest paths from sss to all vertices vvv.

Note that if some vertices are unreachable from the starting vertex sss, the values d[v]d[v]d[v] for them will remain infinite. Obviously, the last few iterations of the algorithm will choose those vertices, but no useful work will be done for them. Therefore, the algorithm can be stopped as soon as the selected vertex has infinite distance to it.

Restoring Shortest Paths

Usually one needs to know not only the lengths of shortest paths but also the shortest paths themselves. Let's see how to maintain sufficient information to restore the shortest path from sss to any vertex. We'll maintain an array of predecessors p[]p[]p[] in which for each vertex v≠sv \ne sv=s, p[v]p[v]p[v] is the penultimate vertex in the shortest path from sss to vvv. Here we use the fact that if we take the shortest path to some vertex vvv and remove vvv from this path, we'll get a path ending in at vertex p[v]p[v]p[v], and this path will be the shortest for the vertex p[v]p[v]p[v]. This array of predecessors can be used to restore the shortest path to any vertex: starting with vvv, repeatedly take the predecessor of the current vertex until we reach the starting vertex sss to get the required shortest path with vertices listed in reverse order. So, the shortest path PPP to the vertex vvv is equal to:

P=(s,…,p[p[p[v]]],p[p[v]],p[v],v)P = (s, \ldots, p[p[p[v]]], p[p[v]], p[v], v)P=(s,…,p[p[p[v]]],p[p[v]],p[v],v)

Building this array of predecessors is very simple: for each successful relaxation, i.e. when for some selected vertex vvv, there is an improvement in the distance to some vertex to\text{to}to, we update the predecessor vertex for to\text{to}to with vertex vvv:

p[to]=vp[\text{to}] = vp[to]=v

Proof

The main assertion on which Dijkstra's algorithm correctness is based is the following:

After any vertex vvv becomes marked, the current distance to it d[v]d[v]d[v] is the shortest, and will no longer change.

The proof is done by induction. For the first iteration this statement is obvious: the only marked vertex is sss, and the distance to is d[s]=0d[s] = 0d[s]=0 is indeed the length of the shortest path to sss. Now suppose this statement is true for all previous iterations, i.e. for all already marked vertices; let's prove that it is not violated after the current iteration completes. Let vvv be the vertex selected in the current iteration, i.e. vvv is the vertex that the algorithm will mark. Now we have to prove that d[v]d[v]d[v] is indeed equal to the length of the shortest path to it l[v]l[v]l[v].

Consider the shortest path PPP to the vertex vvv. This path can be split into two parts: P1P_1P1​ which consists of only marked nodes (at least the starting vertex sss is part of P1P_1P1​), and the rest of the path P2P_2P2​ (it may include a marked vertex, but it always starts with an unmarked vertex). Let's denote the first vertex of the path P2P_2P2​ as ppp, and the last vertex of the path P1P_1P1​ as qqq.

First we prove our statement for the vertex ppp, i.e. let's prove that d[p]=l[p]d[p] = l[p]d[p]=l[p]. This is almost obvious: on one of the previous iterations we chose the vertex qqq and performed relaxation from it. Since (by virtue of the choice of vertex ppp) the shortest path to ppp is the shortest path to qqq plus edge (p,q)(p,q)(p,q), the relaxation from qqq set the value of d[p]d[p]d[p] to the length of the shortest path l[p]l[p]l[p].

Since the edges' weights are non-negative, the length of the shortest path l[p]l[p]l[p] (which we just proved to be equal to d[p]d[p]d[p]) does not exceed the length l[v]l[v]l[v] of the shortest path to the vertex vvv. Given that l[v]≤d[v]l[v] \le d[v]l[v]≤d[v] (because Dijkstra's algorithm could not have found a shorter way than the shortest possible one), we get the inequality:

d[p]=l[p]≤l[v]≤d[v]d[p] = l[p] \le l[v] \le d[v]d[p]=l[p]≤l[v]≤d[v]

On the other hand, since both vertices ppp and vvv are unmarked, and the current iteration chose vertex vvv, not ppp, we get another inequality:

d[p]≥d[v]d[p] \ge d[v]d[p]≥d[v]

From these two inequalities we conclude that d[p]=d[v]d[p] = d[v]d[p]=d[v], and then from previously found equations we get:

d[v]=l[v]d[v] = l[v]d[v]=l[v]

Q.E.D.

Implementation

Dijkstra's algorithm performs nnn iterations. On each iteration it selects an unmarked vertex vvv with the lowest value d[v]d[v]d[v], marks it and checks all the edges (v,to)(v, \text{to})(v,to) attempting to improve the value d[to]d[\text{to}]d[to].

The running time of the algorithm consists of:

  • nnn searches for a vertex with the smallest value d[v]d[v]d[v] among O(n)O(n)O(n) unmarked vertices
  • mmm relaxation attempts

For the simplest implementation of these operations on each iteration vertex search requires O(n)O(n)O(n) operations, and each relaxation can be performed in O(1)O(1)O(1). Hence, the resulting asymptotic behavior of the algorithm is:

O(n2+m)O(n^2+m)O(n2+m)

This complexity is optimal for dense graph, i.e. when m≈n2m \approx n^2m≈n2. However in sparse graphs, when mmm is much smaller than the maximal number of edges n2n^2n2, the problem can be solved in O(nlog⁡n+m)O(n \log n + m)O(nlogn+m) complexity. The algorithm and implementation can be found on the article Dijkstra on sparse graphs.

const int INF = 1000000000;
vector<vector<pair<int, int>>> adj;

void dijkstra(int s, vector<int> & d, vector<int> & p) {
    int n = adj.size();
    d.assign(n, INF);
    p.assign(n, -1);
    vector<bool> u(n, false);

    d[s] = 0;
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        int v = -1;
        for (int j = 0; j < n; j++) {
            if (!u[j] && (v == -1 || d[j] < d[v]))
                v = j;
        }
        
        if (d[v] == INF)
            break;
        
        u[v] = true;
        for (auto edge : adj[v]) {
            int to = edge.first;
            int len = edge.second;
            
            if (d[v] + len < d[to]) {
                d[to] = d[v] + len;
                p[to] = v;
            }
        }
    }
}

Here the graph adj\text{adj}adj is stored as adjacency list: for each vertex vvv adj[v]\text{adj}[v]adj[v] contains the list of edges going from this vertex, i.e. the list of pair<int,int> where the first element in the pair is the vertex at the other end of the edge, and the second element is the edge weight.

The function takes the starting vertex sss and two vectors that will be used as return values.

First of all, the code initializes arrays: distances d[]d[]d[], labels u[]u[]u[] and predecessors p[]p[]p[]. Then it performs nnn iterations. At each iteration the vertex vvv is selected which has the smallest distance d[v]d[v]d[v] among all the unmarked vertices. If the distance to selected vertex vvv is equal to infinity, the algorithm stops. Otherwise the vertex is marked, and all the edges going out from this vertex are checked. If relaxation along the edge is possible (i.e. distance d[to]d[\text{to}]d[to] can be improved), the distance d[to]d[\text{to}]d[to] and predecessor p[to]p[\text{to}]p[to] are updated.

After performing all the iterations array d[]d[]d[] stores the lengths of the shortest paths to all vertices, and array p[]p[]p[] stores the predecessors of all vertices (except starting vertex sss). The path to any vertex ttt can be restored in the following way:

vector<int> restore_path(int s, int t, vector<int> const& p) {
    vector<int> path;

    for (int v = t; v != s; v = p[v])
        path.push_back(v);
    path.push_back(s);

    reverse(path.begin(), path.end());
    return path;
}
